text:
Education in Nigeria follows a structured yet evolving system, shaped by both colonial and post-colonial policies. The **6-3-3-4 system** (six years of primary, three years of junior secondary, three years of senior secondary, and four years of tertiary education) was introduced in 1976, later revised to the **9-3-4 system** (nine years of primary, three years of junior secondary, and four years of tertiary education). Primary education is free and compulsory for children aged 5–12, while secondary education is divided into Junior Secondary School (JSS) and Senior Secondary School (SSS), with students taking the **Senior Secondary Certificate Examination (SSCE)** at the end of SSS.
The **West African Examination Council (WAEC)** administers SSCE, alongside the **National Examination Council (NECO)** , with a grading system ranging from A1 (best) to F9 (fail). Tertiary education is dominated by public universities (e.g., University of Ibadan, University of Lagos), which are majority-controlled by the federal government, alongside private universities. Vocational education, managed by the **National Board for Technical Education (NBTE)** , is also a key component, though challenges like outdated curricula and teacher shortages persist.
**Universal Basic Education (UBE)** , established in 1999, aims to provide free, compulsory, and accessible education for all children aged 6–14, though implementation remains uneven. Female education faces barriers such as poverty, religious beliefs, and insecurity, with efforts like the **Girls’ Education Project (GEP3-CTP)** by UNICEF addressing these issues. Rural areas often lack infrastructure and qualified teachers, exacerbating disparities. Despite progress, Nigeria’s literacy rate remains low (69% as of 2024), with significant regional disparities, particularly in the North-East and North-West. The government continues to prioritize literacy and digital education initiatives to improve accessibility and quality.
